name: La Tène culture
title: The story of the La Tène culture

text: About 2,400 years ago, the La Tène culture spread across much of Europe from north of the Alps.
It is named after a place on Lake Neuchâtel, in Switzerland, where thousands of objects were left in the water.
src: The La Tène culture followed the Hallstatt culture without a definite break about 450 BCE and spread from its core north of the Alps across much of Europe
The La Tène culture is named after its type site on the north shore of Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland, where thousands of objects had been deposited in the lake.

text: Greek and Roman writers called these people Celts and Gauls.
Kings and nobles led them, and once, at Bibracte, they chose Vercingetorix as their war leader against Rome.
src: Its people were those whom Greek and Roman writers called Celts and Gauls
Peoples were divided into tribes, usually ruled by kings / Society was ranked, with nobles / as an assembly of Gauls at Bibracte chose Vercingetorix against Rome

text: Their priests, the Druids, were also judges, healers and teachers.
People left offerings in lakes and rivers, and in deep pits.
src: The Druids were religious leaders and also judges, keepers of lore, healers and political advisers / teachers of natural philosophy, astronomy and mathematics
La Tène peoples dug ritual shafts into which votive offerings and even human sacrifices were cast, and made offerings in lakes and rivers

text: Their metal workers decorated shields, helmets and neck rings called torcs with curling spirals.
Celtic craftsmen are also credited with wooden barrels held together by hoops.
src: intricate spirals and interlace, inscribed and inlaid, on fine bronze vessels, helmets, shields, horse trappings and elite jewellery, above all the neck rings called torcs
Celtic craftsmen are credited with shrunk-on iron tyres, wagons with front-axle steering, roller bearings in wheel hubs and wooden barrels bound with hoops

text: They traded salt, tin, furs and gold to the south for wine and fine goods.
Rich graves, like the Vix Grave in France, hold treasures brought from far away.
src: Salt, tin, copper, amber, wool, leather, furs and gold went south, and wine, luxuries and coral came north.
early La Tène elite burials such as the Vix Grave in Burgundy hold imported luxuries

text: More than 2,000 years ago, the Roman general Julius Caesar conquered Gaul.
Many of their walled towns became Roman cities, and one of them, Lutetia, is now Paris.
src: 58–50 BCE: Julius Caesar’s Gallic Wars complete the Roman conquest of Gaul
From the 2nd century BCE walled towns, the oppida, appeared / A significant number of oppida became Roman cities, among them Vesontio (Besançon), Durocortorum (Reims), Lutetia (Paris)
